entry.title: Graded by the tower they build: a game-based assessment of civil engineering graduate attributes for accreditation at a Costa Rican university (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Costa Rica's Civil Engineering School designed a tower-construction game-based assessment and ran it at three curricular stages (initial, intermediate and advanced) in the degree programme. Observable performance indicators from 28 student teams, more than 110 students in all, were normalised to 0-100 scores covering five graduate attributes: design and development, environment and sustainability, teamwork, problem analysis, and project administration and finances. Design and development, environment and sustainability, and teamwork improved significantly across the three stages, problem analysis stayed stable, and a student survey found high clarity and fairness.

Why it matters here: This is a rare case of gamified assessment used for formal programme-level accreditation evidence rather than for teaching alone, which speaks directly to the diversified-assessment strand of the Wits study: a hands-on building task scored against named graduate attributes could be adapted to generate comparable evidence of what students actually grasp about structure-property relationships, alongside the surveys and classroom observation already planned.

Mata Abdelnour, Cruz-Zuñiga and Centeno Mora, Quality Assurance in Education, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, ahead of print, subscription access (Emerald Publishing)

entry.title: AI turns calculus review sheets into arcade-style games for engineering students at a Guatemalan university (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Engineering lecturers at Universidad Galileo in Guatemala used AI tools to turn conventional calculus review worksheets into 'Fun Study Guides': browser-based, HTML5 game prototypes with timers, score counters and ranking tables. Three prototypes are described, Multivariable Calculus: Arcade Challenge, Integral Invaders and Quantico: Numerical Mission, covering multivariable calculus and numerical methods such as root finding, interpolation and numerical integration. The paper, presented at the 2026 ASEE Annual Conference in Charlotte, sets out the design and build process but reports no student evaluation data yet.

Why it matters here: This is a direct, low-cost template for the 'AI-generated or AI-mediated games' strand named in the Wits project brief: lecturers, not programmers, used AI tools to convert their own existing worksheets into games, which is exactly the kind of co-design the Wits study's workshops could test for turning crystallography or phase-transformation problem sheets into quick digital games.

Cotto, Alvarado and Portillo, 2026 ASEE Annual Conference and Exposition · Peer-reviewed conference paper (ASEE Annual Conference proceedings), open access via the ASEE PEER repository

entry.title: An Erasmus+ project trains 40 lecturers across five African countries to lead teacher education for sustainable development (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Leuphana Universität Lüneburg leads an Erasmus+ capacity-building project on teacher leadership for education for sustainable development, working with universities in South Africa, Zambia, Namibia, Malawi and Kenya alongside partners in Germany, Cyprus and Greece. By May 2026 the project had completed a Training of Trainers programme producing 40 trained lecturers able to teach education for sustainable development leadership courses and guide colleagues in running education for sustainable development change projects. The University of the Witwatersrand leads the scaling of these change projects jointly with the University of Malawi.

Why it matters here: The University of the Witwatersrand already runs an international Erasmus+ consortium role here, leading change-project scaling jointly with the University of Malawi, so the Wits School of Education can draw directly on its own cascade model, the Training of Trainers approach that turned 40 lecturers into in-house trainers, when preparing staff and candidates for the Aix-Marseille exchange.

Hülsmann, M., Leuphana Universität Lüneburg news, 2026 · University news article, institutional source (Leuphana Universität Lüneburg), reporting on an active Erasmus+-funded capacity-building project

entry.title: University of Sharjah builds an explainable dropout early-warning system from a decade of UAE STEM enrolment records (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Sharjah built an explainable machine-learning early-warning system to flag dropout risk among undergraduate STEM students in the MENA region, using longitudinal data from 6,798 students at a major UAE university spanning ten cohorts from 2010 to 2019. Of six classifiers tested on routine student information system records, XGBoost, Gradient Boosting Machine and Random Forest performed best, each reaching an AUC-ROC above 0.91 and an F1-score above 0.84, with withdrawn semesters, second-term credit load, academic probation history and mathematics and physics performance the strongest predictors. The authors applied SHAP analysis to make the model's predictions interpretable at both the whole-population and individual-student level, and note the system needs no external surveys or learning-management-system data, only data already held by the registrar.

Why it matters here: PASS can test the same combination the Sharjah team used, routine student-system records plus SHAP explainability, as a benchmark against models trained on anonymised Wits School of Education data, and borrow its use of withdrawn semesters and credit load as predictors that a Business Intelligence Services dataset is likely to hold too.

Al Hashmi, Zervopoulos, Elmehdi and Ozturk, Emerging Science Journal, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Aix-Marseille's own teacher-training institute launches a plurilingualism-and-AI exchange with Dakar's teacher training centre (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Aix-Marseille Université's INSPE and the Centre Régional de Formation des Personnels de l'Éducation (CRFPE) of Dakar launched a teaching and teacher-training cooperation project on 14 November 2025, supported by the French Embassy in Senegal. The launch set up two collaborative workspaces in Senegal, one on plurilingualism and artificial intelligence and one on fablab and artificial intelligence, to share experiences and co-construct teaching resources suited to local contexts. In March 2026 ten student teachers from the Dakar CRFPE are due to visit the Aix-Marseille INSPE to take courses and meet primary school pupils.

Why it matters here: Aix-Marseille's INSPE is the lead partner in the Erasmus+ KA171-HED project with Wits, and this Dakar exchange shows the same institute already running a bilingual, AI-themed teacher-training partnership with a Global South partner, a tested workspace format and a direct institutional contact for lessons on plurilingual content and for twinning the Wits mobility cohorts with a comparable Francophone West African partner.

Aix-Marseille Université, INSPE · Institutional programme page, Aix-Marseille Université INSPE (official partner institution), reporting the project's launch

entry.title: A smartphone's journey as a quiz game: a Horizon Europe critical raw materials game built with a Zambian partner university (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
AGEMERA, a three-year Horizon Europe project coordinated by the University of Oulu in Finland with the University of Zambia among its 19 partners across 11 countries, published a free online serious game on critical raw materials. Modelled on the 'Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?' quiz format, the 20-question game follows a smartphone through extraction, processing, manufacturing, use and recycling, and is offered in several languages including Finnish, English, German, Spanish, Estonian and Romanian, as part of a wider educational package aimed at schools and universities. The project also mapped roughly 4,700 square kilometres of ground for critical raw materials across six EU states and Zambia.

Why it matters here: AGEMERA shows how a mining and metals supply chain, the raw material end of the structure-property chain the Wits study teaches, can be turned into a simple, freely reusable quiz game with a named African university as a genuine research partner rather than just a study site; its multi-language, schools-and-universities educational package is a workable model for the Wits team's own materials beyond the laboratory.

Joutsenvaara, University of Oulu Kerttu Saalasti Institute Blog, 2025 · Institutional blog post and project webpage from a Horizon Europe-funded research project, freely accessible online, not independently peer-reviewed

entry.title: Two advising algorithms built on the same state community college system send fewer at-risk Black students the extra help they need (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Virginia examined two prediction models, one for course completion and one for degree completion, built on system-wide administrative records from the Virginia Community College System covering 2007 to 2019. They found that if either model were used to target extra support at "at-risk" students, algorithmic bias would mean fewer marginal Black students received that support than White students, and that the size of the bias changed depending on whether "at-risk" was defined as the bottom decile or the bottom half of predicted scores. They trace part of the bias to the administrative data being less predictive of Black students' success than of White students' success, particularly for new students, and suggest that collecting more data could narrow the gap.

Why it matters here: A direct warning for PASS before any model goes near the University's Business Intelligence Services data: reporting one overall accuracy figure is not enough, the same model can send support to fewer at-risk Black or minoritised students depending only on how "at-risk" is defined, and the fix may be collecting more predictive data on under-served groups rather than adjusting the algorithm after the fact.

Bird, Castleman and Song, Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (subscription access, Wiley)

entry.title: A simple decision tree built from two years of enrolment records flags dropout risk at a Malaysian private university (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Universiti Utara Malaysia, working with Oman's Ministry of Education, extracted 7,706 student records from a Malaysian private university's database covering the 2018 to 2019 intake to test decision tree and logistic regression classifiers for predicting dropout. After testing several data partitions, decision tree variants and logistic regression imputation methods, they found a chi-square decision tree with two branches performed best, reaching 89.49 percent accuracy on an 80/20 train-test split, and the chosen model also identified the variables most useful for predicting dropout. The authors frame dropout as a threat to university enrolment, revenue and student wellbeing, and argue the model could help flag at-risk students early.

Why it matters here: A directly comparable scale and data type to PASS's own starting point: a single institution's own enrolment records, modest classifiers rather than deep learning, and a result, 89.49 percent accuracy from a simple decision tree, that sets a realistic early benchmark for what anonymised Wits School of Education data alone might achieve before Business Intelligence Services data is added.

Roslan, Mohd Jamil, Mohd Shaharanee and Sultan Alawi, Journal of Advanced Research in Applied Sciences and Engineering Technology, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY-NC 4.0)

entry.title: Parma's Erasmus+ KA171-HED fund gives extreme priority to the most disadvantaged staff and students from Rwanda, Senegal and Niger (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The University of Parma's Centre for International University Cooperation (CUCI) was awarded an Erasmus+ KA171-HED fund supporting academic mobility with universities in Rwanda, Senegal and Niger. The fund covers 21 incoming teaching-staff positions, who take three-week laboratory training courses and summer schools updating pedagogical methods, and 19 incoming student places for three to four month internships. Selection explicitly requires gender balance and gives extreme priority to the most economically disadvantaged students and teaching staff from the partner countries.

Why it matters here: This KA171-HED consortium shows a concrete, publicly stated equity rule, explicit gender balance and extreme priority for the most disadvantaged applicants, for selecting incoming teaching staff and structuring their pedagogical training, a model the Wits and Aix-Marseille partnership could adapt when it sets its own selection criteria for master's, doctoral and staff mobility cohorts.

Università di Parma (CUCI) · Institutional announcement page, Università di Parma (official recipient institution of the Erasmus+ KA171-HED award)

entry.title: Four South African universities, 30 staff and a Big Data framework for retention: Fort Hare maps the data and ethics gaps (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Fort Hare interviewed 30 academic staff members across four South African public universities and analysed institutional retention reports, policy documents and strategic plans, using an interpretivist qualitative approach supported by Design Science. They found fragmented data systems, limited data literacy among staff and concerns about the ethical use of data, alongside a stated need for predictive analytics, integrated data systems and personalised support. From this they propose a Big Data framework meant to move universities from reactive to proactive retention management through ethical data governance, integrated data processing, predictive analytics and personalised interventions.

Why it matters here: This study names the obstacles PASS must work through with the University's Business Intelligence Services before any model reaches advisers: data spread across separate systems, staff unused to reading risk data and worries about its ethical use. Its framework offers a checklist for the governance and staff-capacity side of PASS, which a purely technical model would miss.

Mainoti and Piderit, South African Journal of Information Management, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0)

entry.title: Moroccan researchers argue for virtual exchange built into English teacher education, not as a stand-in for travel (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
This paper by researchers at Sidi Mohammed Ben Abdellah University in Fes and Mohammed First University in Oujda examines virtual exchange as a practical form of internationalisation at home in Moroccan teacher education for teachers of English as a foreign language. Drawing on a narrative review of research on internationalisation, virtual exchange and intercultural learning, it argues that virtual exchange is not a simple digital substitute for physical mobility but a structured, guided and reflective pedagogy. It proposes a pathway in which virtual exchange embedded in the curriculum puts internationalisation at home into practice and creates conditions for future teachers to develop intercultural literacy.

Why it matters here: Only some Wits School of Education and INSPE Aix-Marseille students and staff will travel under the grant, and this North African case for embedding virtual exchange in the teacher education curriculum suggests how the partnership could reach the rest, for instance through shared online modules on multilingual teaching before and after each physical stay. Being conceptual, it offers a design to test rather than measured outcomes.

Abdellaoui and Zerrik, Journal of Interdisciplinary Studies in Education, 15(6), 129-150, 2026 · Journal article, open access (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); a conceptual paper based on a narrative literature review

entry.title: Tokyo University of Technology builds an early-warning model meant to survive the move to a new academic year (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Tokyo University of Technology note that Japan's declining birthrate is widening the spread of academic ability among university students, making it crucial to identify students at risk of academic failure early. They present an early-warning system, built on learning-management-system data, that combines data augmentation with a transfer-learning classification model drawing on Transformer and XGBoost, designed for small samples and for the shift in student data from one academic year to the next. The authors report that it achieved the best overall performance against a conventional predictive model, that its stability was confirmed with the hold-out method, and that all data were collected without identifiable information.

Why it matters here: A PASS model trained on past Wits School of Education cohorts will meet the same difficulty when it is applied to a new intake: small programme-level samples and student populations that shift from year to year. This study offers a method to borrow for checking that a PASS model still holds in the next academic year, and a reminder to work with non-identifiable data from the start.

Tan, She, Chen, Ohno and Kameda, Journal of Advanced Computational Intelligence and Intelligent Informatics, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Fuji Technology Press)

entry.title: Metallmani: a printable board game in which chemical engineering students run their own metal-producing company and pay CO2 taxes (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Teachers at NTNU designed Metallmani, a board game in which each player manages a company in the metallurgical industry, buying raw materials, investing in processing plants, paying to run the processes, selling products and dealing with CO2 taxes and other societal issues. It was played every autumn from 2021 to 2024 in IMAK2002 Inorganic Chemistry, a compulsory second-year course for bachelor chemical engineering students, in groups of 3 or 4 per board and in sessions of about 90 minutes including the rules and a wrap-up. Of the 50 students who played, 45 answered a survey: over 90% said they liked the game and most said it gave them a better overview of metallurgical processes and of their raw materials, waste and emissions, although fewer agreed that it was educational than that it was fun.

Why it matters here: Metallmani is one of very few board games built specifically for metallurgy, and every component is printed on paper, which makes it a low-cost model for the board games the Wits study is testing in metallurgical engineering. Its candid finding that students rated the game more fun than educational is a useful warning for the Wits team's surveys and classroom observation: enjoyment and learning need to be measured separately.

Aakre, Tokle, Vik and Kleveland, Nordic Journal of STEM Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Teaching Tool section), open access under CC BY 4.0; written in Norwegian with an English abstract

entry.title: A Swiss teacher education department sends trainee teachers on two-month placements in Kenya, Togo and Ghana (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Since 2011 the Department of Education and Learning and University of Teacher Education (DFA/ASP) of SUPSI in Switzerland has run a mobility programme that places trainee teachers in schools and other educational settings abroad for two months; relaunched in 2022/23 as "Experiencing school elsewhere", its 2024-2025 destinations included Costa Rica, Kenya, Togo and Ghana. The module combines a preparatory phase on intercultural skills and comparative school systems, a field phase accompanied by local professionals, and a concluding phase assessed through an interview and a multimedia product; 44 participants had taken part between 2011 and June 2025. Most described the experience as transformative, while the difficulties they reported included the emotional impact of profound social inequalities, unforeseen events and misunderstandings over communication habits.

Why it matters here: This is a working model of short, structured placements for student teachers in African schools, with preparation, local mentoring and assessed reflection, which the Wits School of Education and INSPE Aix-Marseille could adapt for master's students in bilingual teaching. Its candid list of difficulties, from the emotional weight of inequality to misread communication codes, is a useful checklist for preparing students who will move in both directions between South Africa and France.

SUPSI Newsroom, 23 June 2025 · University newsroom article (interview with the programme coordinator)

entry.title: Spanish bilingual student teachers who took part in international programmes rate their intercultural and plurilingual competence higher (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
A questionnaire survey of 99 bilingual pre-service teachers at four public universities in Spain measured their self-perceived intercultural and plurilingual competences against gender, schooling in a bilingual primary track, participation in international programmes and language proficiency. Mann-Whitney U tests indicated that both competences seem linked to participation in international programmes and to language proficiency, while bilingual primary schooling had a weak effect and no gender differences were found. The two competences were positively correlated.

Why it matters here: The project's master's mobility is for students in bilingual teaching, and this study links international programme participation to bilingual student teachers' view of their own intercultural and plurilingual competence, which suggests what the Wits School of Education and INSPE Aix-Marseille could measure before and after each exchange. As a self-report survey with no follow-up over time, it shows an association rather than proof that mobility causes the gain.

Arnaiz-Castro, Gómez-Parra and Espejo, Revista Interuniversitaria de Formación del Profesorado, 99(38.3), 63-84, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 ES)

entry.title: Assessed by the game they build: engineers on a Tunisian master's programme design serious games as their module assessment (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
In the first semester of 2022/2023, a lecturer at the University of Tunis assessed two master's groups of 20 students each through serious games they designed on the module's own content; in the Business Games module of the Innovation master's at the National Engineering School of Tunis, where most students were working engineers, the games were built in Scratch. Among respondents from the engineering group, 78% said they revised the course material to build the game and 78% that they mastered the chapters better than with classic revision, 87% appreciated being assessed this way and 30% said it took more time than revising for an exam. The experiment was repeated in 2023/2024 at the students' request.

Why it matters here: The Wits study asks whether assessment beyond the exam helps engineering students learn, and here the game itself becomes the assessment task, with criteria announced at the start of the semester that rewarded workplace scenarios over simple quizzes. It offers a North African model the Wits team could adapt in its co-design workshops, asking metallurgy students to build a game on crystallography or phase transformations and marking it against the course outcomes.

Sellami, Heliyon, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; small questionnaire study with two groups of 20 students

entry.title: Brazil's State University of Maringá tests enrolment-only dropout prediction at scale (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the State University of Maringá in Brazil evaluated Decision Tree, Random Forest and XGBoost models against enrolment records for 66,820 undergraduate students across 45 programmes from 2002 to 2022. Using only static, enrolment-time variables and a temporal validation split to control information leakage, XGBoost reached a PR-AUC of 0.586 against a dropout prevalence of 0.364, about 1.6 times random performance. Accuracy fell when a model trained on older cohorts was tested on newer ones, a decline the authors attribute to calibration shift rather than worse risk ranking, which they show can be corrected by adjusting the decision threshold without retraining.

Why it matters here: PASS also starts from existing institutional records rather than new survey data, so this large, long-run Brazilian dataset is a useful comparator for how much predictive power enrolment-time variables alone can offer, and a reminder to monitor and recalibrate any Wits model as cohorts change from year to year.

Mincache, Catharin, Teixeira, Colanzi, da Costa and Feltrim, Technologies, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Greek university's 2026 Erasmus+ KA171 call results add a first South African partner (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
In its August 2026 call results announcement, Hellenic Mediterranean University reported an Erasmus+ KA171 grant of 247,577 euros (agreement 2026-1-EL01-KA171-HED-000442730) funding 66 mobility places across 68 partner universities in 22 countries, made up of 42 staff and 24 student mobilities. The 2026 round added twelve new partner institutions, including, for the first time, South Africa's Durban University of Technology, alongside institutions in the Western Balkans, the Mediterranean region and the Neighbourhood East.

Why it matters here: As a European KA171 grant holder running the same European Commission funding instrument as the Wits-Aix-Marseille project, Hellenic Mediterranean University's published figures give the administrative staff coordinating the Wits-Aix-Marseille exchange a useful benchmark of typical grant size and mobility numbers.

Hellenic Mediterranean University International Relations Office, 2026 · University international relations office programme page

entry.title: South Africa to Uganda benchmarking visit on teacher assessment and curriculum reform (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
In July 2026 a delegation of 24 officials from Uganda's Ministry of Education and Sports visited Tshwane University of Technology's Soshanguve South campus in South Africa to benchmark teacher assessment and curriculum reform practices. The visit focused on formative and summative assessment approaches for competency-based education, and Tshwane University of Technology was noted as one of only a few institutions on the continent offering a comprehensive four-year assessment programme for student teachers. The two sides discussed establishing a memorandum of understanding on teacher education and inclusive education reform.

Why it matters here: This shows a comparable model of staff benchmarking and curriculum and assessment exchange in teacher education, from which the Wits School of Education's Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille's INSPE can draw lessons, particularly for the administrative staff who will organise joint training visits.

Tshwane University of Technology newsroom, 2026 · University newsroom article

entry.title: A physical and online escape room that teaches engineering mechanics and material behaviour through linked puzzles (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
A team led by Professor Christina Vollmecke at TU Berlin's Chair of Stability and Failure of Functionally Optimized Structures built GAMEchanics, described as the first escape room themed entirely on engineering mechanics. Players solve six linked puzzle stations covering topics such as material strength, the right-hand rule and column buckling, in both a physical pop-up room and an online version built with the Godot engine. The one-year project was funded by the Klaus Tschira Foundation, was first shown publicly at the TU Berlin Long Night of the Sciences in June 2024, and its puzzle designs and setup guide are published openly on GitHub under a CC BY-NC licence.

Why it matters here: GAMEchanics is a ready-made, openly licensed template for turning structure-property and materials-behaviour content into a physical or digital escape room, exactly the kind of beyond-the-exam assessment format the Wits AHEAD study wants to test with metallurgical engineering students. Its explicit goal of lowering the barrier to engineering for under-represented groups also matches the project's interest in who gamification reaches.

Vollmecke, Donitz, Kurpjuhn and Jacobi, Proceedings in Applied Mathematics and Mechanics, 2026 · Peer-reviewed conference proceedings article (GAMM Annual Meeting), with an open-source repository

entry.title: A Guess Who style structure-drawing game used to build first-year chemistry students' communication skills and community (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Chemistry lecturers at Newcastle University created CHEMmunicate, a low-tech game in which one student describes a mystery chemical structure for a teammate to draw on a whiteboard, using only yes or no answers to questions from the rest of the team. It was run across eight Senior Tutor Check-In sessions of about 12 to 16 first-year undergraduates each, reaching over 200 students in the 2024/2025 academic year, and was evaluated with questionnaires and focus group discussions. More than 90 percent of students agreed that they had enjoyed the session, felt more confident describing chemical structures, and would approach their tutors more comfortably afterwards.

Why it matters here: CHEMmunicate shows how a simple, low-tech game, evaluated with the same questionnaire-plus-focus-group approach the Wits AHEAD study plans to use, can turn abstract structural reasoning into a sociable classroom activity for first-year students. It is a method worth trialling for teaching crystal structures before more complex gamified digital tools are introduced.

Navarro Reguero and Hopkinson, Journal of Chemical Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Two serious role-playing video games used to review thermodynamics and heat transfer in a Spanish engineering degree (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Cadiz built two role-playing video games using RPG Maker to help engineering students review thermodynamics and heat transfer in the Thermotechnics subject. In the 2022/2023 academic year, 288 students played the first game and 252 played the second, out of 370 students enrolled across six engineering degree programmes. Students who played the games achieved higher academic scores, reported increased motivation and a reduced perceived complexity of the subject, and prior gaming experience did not significantly affect the games' impact.

Why it matters here: The quasi-experimental design, with pre- and post-game surveys and a direct comparison of game players' exam scores against the rest of the cohort, gives the Wits AHEAD team a tested method for measuring whether board games and digital games actually move marks in a technical subject, not just enjoyment. The subject matter is also close to home, since thermodynamics and heat transfer sit alongside phase transformations in a materials and metallurgical curriculum.

Romero Rodriguez, Sanchez-Alzola and Salazar, Computer Applications in Engineering Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: CIVIS seed funding scheme for joint African-European research, linking Wits and Aix-Marseille directly (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
CIVIS, the European University Alliance of eleven European and six African universities including Aix-Marseille University and the University of the Witwatersrand, ran a seed funding call for African-European research collaborations that opened on 25 March 2025 and closed on 31 May 2025, covering activities such as doctoral schools, workshops and joint grant-writing visits. Each selected project could receive up to 10,000 euros, with staff mobility costs covered up to 850 euros within Europe and 1,500 euros between Europe and Africa, and funded projects had to be completed by 30 June 2026.

Why it matters here: This CIVIS seed funding scheme directly links Aix-Marseille University and the University of the Witwatersrand as fellow alliance members, giving Wits School of Education and Wits International a concrete, existing funding route to extend the Erasmus+ mobility into joint doctoral schools and research visits with Aix-Marseille beyond the KA171 grant itself.

CIVIS European University Alliance call page, 2025 · European University Alliance funding call page

entry.title: Brazilian and Chilean universities flag at-risk students from weekly Moodle activity (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Building on the LANSE learning-analytics platform, researchers from universities in Brazil and Chile trained a CatBoost model on Moodle log data covering 567 student-course instances across 23 courses, using 25 engagement and access features with NSGA-II hyperparameter optimisation and ADASYN resampling. A single model trained on relative course-progression data outperformed separate week-by-week models, reaching an F1-score of 0.86, recall of 0.85, accuracy of 0.90 and an AUC of 0.95 for at-risk students by week 7. The study compared weekly against unified modelling strategies rather than reporting only one model's accuracy.

Why it matters here: PASS could trial a similar Moodle log-based, within-course early-warning layer alongside its enrolment-record models, since this shows that activity data collected automatically during a course can flag at-risk students well before final grades are available.

Marcolino, Porto, Primo, Targino, Ramos, Queiroga, Munoz and Cechinel, Scientific Reports, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (Nature Scientific Reports), open access

entry.title: Italy's University of Catania predicts undergraduate dropout with XGBoost (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Catania built a dropout prediction model from five years of historical records covering 42,000 undergraduate students across the university's departments. They compared logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost and a neural network to classify students as continuing or dropping out, and XGBoost reached 97 percent accuracy, with random forest close behind at 94 percent. The underlying data remain the university's own property, restricted to its data analysis office.

Why it matters here: This shows how far accuracy can go with routine administrative records alone at university scale, a useful benchmark as PASS moves from its Wits School of Education pilot data towards models built with the University's Business Intelligence Services.

Miracula, Mazzeo Rinaldi and Giuffrida, LOD 2024 conference proceedings (Springer), 2025 · Peer-reviewed conference proceedings (Springer Lecture Notes in Computer Science)

entry.title: A board game in first-year engineering: two Colombian universities use it to teach ethics (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Pontificia Universidad Javeriana adapted the commercial board game Sheriff of Nottingham into a 90-minute engineering-entrepreneurship session with asymmetric roles, negotiation, consequences and a structured debriefing, and ran it in 17 first-semester engineering course offerings at two Colombian universities. Across 616 questionnaires before and 413 after, the overall ethical-awareness score rose from 7.40 to 8.79 in the 2025-1 semester, and in 2025-2 90.4% of students agreed that the game helped them reflect differently on ethical dilemmas. The authors state that the unmatched samples and the lack of a comparison group rule out causal claims.

Why it matters here: The design is the part to borrow: a short board-game session with a structured debriefing, run across many first-year engineering sections, is close to what the Wits metallurgy study plans for crystallography and phase transformations. Its stated limits (unmatched before-and-after questionnaires, no comparison group) are a reminder to build a comparison into the Wits classroom design from the start.

Hurtado Londoño, Osorio Rodríguez, Prados and Ivorra Peñafort, Education Sciences, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (Education Sciences, MDPI)

entry.title: steelChallenge-21: a worldwide steelmaking simulation contest to make a steel grade at the lowest cost (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
steeluniversity, the learning programme of the World Steel Association, describes steelChallenge-21 as a game-based blended learning programme in which university students and industry professionals use a combined electric arc furnace and secondary steelmaking simulation to produce a specified steel grade at the lowest cost, supported by online courses, 3D interactive models and practice simulations. Registration opened on 1 September 2026, the 24-hour online regional championship starts on 17 November 2026, and the winner of each category in each of five regions goes to a world championship in Brussels in April 2027. Entry costs €29.99, with 50% academic pricing and volume licences for universities.

Why it matters here: This is the industry-built game closest to metallurgical engineering that the feed has found: a steelmaking simulation that ties process choices to composition and cost, which the Wits team could trial with a class in this year's regional round and observe alongside its own board games. It is not peer-reviewed and publishes no learning outcomes, so any use in the study would rely on the project's own surveys and classroom observation.

steeluniversity, World Steel Association, 2026 · Official programme page of an industry body; not peer-reviewed

entry.title: Teaching mathematics, science and technology in the mother tongue across Africa: a Wits scoping review (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Two Wits School of Education researchers reviewed research published between 2014 and 2025 on mother tongue-based bilingual education in primary mathematics, science and technology across Africa and found 45 outputs that met their criteria, with marked growth in the last six years and a heavy concentration in South Africa. Translanguaging and teacher preparation were the dominant themes, and no research was found on bilingual education in technology education. The authors conclude that the approach works only if teacher preparation is strengthened and classroom practice is brought into line with language-in-education policy.

Why it matters here: The project's master's mobility is for students in bilingual teaching, and this review, written in the Wits School of Education, maps what African research already says on the subject. It gives Wits and INSPE Aix-Marseille a shared starting reading list and points to gaps, such as technology education, that joint work on multilingualism could fill.

Hamukwaya and Essien, South African Journal of Childhood Education, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0)

entry.title: Can Erasmus+ mobility change a teacher? A close study of two teachers in the Netherlands (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the Universidade de Lisboa and Leiden University ran a multiple case study of two teachers in the Netherlands who took part in Erasmus+ Key Action 1 mobility for professional development, using interviews, biographical narratives and focus groups. Mobility prompted deep pedagogical reflection and a rethinking of the teachers' European identity, and the participants linked their personal and professional growth. The authors warn that such mobility succeeds as professional development only when it becomes part of a school-wide improvement strategy rather than an isolated trip.

Why it matters here: The project sends academics and administrative staff as well as students, and this study's warning applies to the Wits School of Education as a sending institution: plan from the start how each returning participant's learning will be shared with colleagues and built into programmes. With only two teachers, it offers ideas to test rather than evidence at scale.

Martins, Alves, Tinoca and Mearns, European Educational Research Journal, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY 4.0)

entry.title: Predicting dropout from a secondary-teacher programme: five Graz cohorts, an admission test and university marks (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Graz built a stacked ensemble model on five cohorts that entered the secondary-teacher bachelor's programme between 2015 and 2019 (2,661 students, of whom 1,124 dropped out), using the TESAT admission test of cognitive and personality measures, demographics and GPA. Admission test and demographics alone reached a mean accuracy of 0.61 and an AUC of 0.62, GPA alone 0.74 and 0.76, and the two combined 0.76 and 0.77. The authors describe the ensemble as a black box and say richer data, such as school grades, are needed before it is used for intervention.

Why it matters here: This is the closest published match to the first setting of PASS: dropout prediction inside an initial teacher education programme. It suggests that university marks carry most of the signal while admission data add little, a result PASS can test on Wits School of Education records, and its caution about black-box models supports PASS's aim of interpretable models built with Business Intelligence Services.

Jud, Weissenbacher and Neubauer, European Journal of Teacher Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)

entry.title: What a three-year KA171 project between Venice and Stellenbosch delivered (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The Venice International University Erasmus+ Mobility Consortium, formed with its Italian member universities, ran a KA171 project with Stellenbosch University from 2022 to 2025 covering long-term and blended student mobility, short doctoral exchanges, and staff teaching and training. Its report records 6 Stellenbosch students on a blended summer session in August 2024 and 3 on a full semester, 16 student and 8 staff mobilities in intensive graduate activities, doctoral exchanges in both directions including one under joint supervision, and administrative staff from each side attending the other's training. Participant surveys gave a weighted average of 88% for students' skills and personal development and 92% for staff's professional skills and growth.

Why it matters here: A South African KA171 partnership that has run its full course, with the same strands as the Wits and Aix-Marseille project: doctoral exchange with joint supervision, staff training for administrators and blended short mobility. Its report shows the modest numbers such projects realistically move and the survey measures a final report uses, a ready template for planning and reporting.

Venice International University, Erasmus+ project report (undated page; activities to July 2025) · Institutional final project report; results self-reported from participant surveys

entry.title: Forecasting next semester's results for 3,093 Ghanaian graduates across 14 degree programmes (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Using anonymised records of 3,093 graduates from the 2015 to 2019 intakes of a public university in Ghana, covering 14 four-year degree programmes and 40 features, the authors predicted each semester's GPA and class from the record up to the previous semester with Random Forest, SVM, LSTM and BiLSTM models. BiLSTM performed best, with classification accuracy rising from 58% in semester 2 to 62% in semester 8, and high-school grades and earlier semester GPAs were the strongest predictors. Because students who dropped out were excluded, the study predicts performance rather than dropout, and its accuracy is modest.

Why it matters here: An African, multi-programme case close to the PASS aim of spotting students likely to take longer to graduate: semester-by-semester forecasting from routine records is a design PASS could compare with one-off dropout models. Its exclusion of dropouts and modest accuracy also show why PASS needs data on students who leave, not only on those who finish.

Diekuu, Mekala, Abonie, Isaacs and Elyan, Cogent Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: Two simple triggers in weeks 3 and 4: how Charles Sturt reaches disengaged first-years before census (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
In semester 1 of 2022 Charles Sturt University monitored 191 first-year units with 15,034 enrolments and, in weeks 3 and 4, flagged students who had not submitted an early low-stakes assessment or showed low activity on the learning platform; an Outreach Team contacted 1,386 flagged students by phone, two-way SMS and other channels. After contact 52% submitted the early assessment, 28% of those contacted came from low socioeconomic backgrounds against 22% across the university, and after a successful conversation retention into the next semester ranged from 64% for students with no equity factors to 75% for those with four or more. The authors note that there was no randomised control group.

Why it matters here: A working model for the intervention side of PASS: explainable triggers that advisers and students can understand, tied to a staffed outreach team and timed before the census date. The Wits team and Business Intelligence Services could adapt it for first-year students in the Wits School of Education and evaluate it with the comparison group this study lacked.

Linden, van der Ploeg and Roman, Journal of Higher Education Policy and Management, 2023 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (evaluation of an institutional programme)

entry.title: Why university teachers hold back from gamification: a systematic review of what drives and blocks it (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
A Bond University team screened 1,096 unique articles from Web of Science, Scopus and EBSCO and included 17 studies of university educators' views on gamification and game-based learning. Educators valued these approaches for interaction, collaboration, fun and engagement, but named lack of time to develop them, lack of proven benefits and classroom setting issues as the main barriers, which the authors group as attitudinal, design-related and administrative. For game-based learning in particular, educators reported little if any proven benefit, and most university educators do not use these approaches routinely.

Why it matters here: A cautionary counterweight for the Wits study: the barriers it names (staff time, doubts about the evidence, room and timetable constraints) are exactly what lecturers in metallurgical engineering are likely to raise, so the project's interviews and co-design workshops can ask about them directly, and its own findings can speak to the 'no proven benefit' objection.

Lester, Skulmoski, Fisher, Mehrotra, Lim, Lang and Keogh, British Journal of Educational Technology, 2023 · Peer-reviewed systematic review (PRISMA), open access

entry.title: Mining Moodle logs in Baltic design courses to catch students about to drop out (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A researcher working with TTK University of Applied Sciences in Estonia and Vilnius Gediminas Technical University in Lithuania analysed 99,104 Moodle activity records from 154 students across six computer-aided design (CAD) courses, focusing on 12,941 logs from 80 students in the two courses with the highest attrition. A random forest model built on a new weighted attribute method, combining engagement, task difficulty and time allocation, reached a cross-validated accuracy of 0.8756, though the author describes the findings as preliminary given the small dataset and calls for external validation.

Why it matters here: Its explicit weighting of time-on-task and task difficulty alongside engagement, drawn straight from Moodle logs, is a practical feature-engineering idea PASS could test on the Wits School of Education's own learning management system data, and its honesty about small-sample limits is a useful caution for early PASS pilots.

Ovtšarenko, Scientific Reports, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (Scientific Reports, Nature Portfolio)

entry.title: Letting engineering students build their own learning games with generative AI (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
In a Software Systems Engineering course at Indiana University Bloomington, students used Microsoft Copilot and other generative AI tools to design and code their own text-based educational games in C, with the project brief and marking rubric themselves partly generated by AI. The published case study, based on students' own design reflections, reports on their design processes, learning gains and the practical and ethical challenges of using generative AI to build games rather than only to answer questions. It frames AI-assisted game design as a way to teach responsible and productive AI use alongside programming.

Why it matters here: This is a direct model for a co-design workshop strand of the Wits study: instead of only playing set games, metallurgical engineering students could use generative AI to help design their own crystallography or phase-transformation games, with the instructor's reflective case-study format offering a template for documenting that process. It also shows how an AI-generated rubric and brief can structure assessment beyond the exam.

Olgun Sadik, International Journal of Designs for Learning, 2025 · Peer-reviewed design case study, open access journal (Indiana University)

entry.title: Twenty-eight institutions across Africa and Europe join forces to fix the teacher shortage (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
The Regional Teachers Initiative for Africa, a 100 million euro European Union programme running from 2024 to 2030 and coordinated by the Finnish National Agency for Education, has launched six research projects (running May 2025 to November 2026) bringing together 28 universities, NGOs and other education institutions from 12 African countries and 6 European countries. The projects work on teacher wellbeing and retention, professional development at scale, early number learning and professional learning communities, with the aim of reducing teacher shortages and attrition and improving teacher motivation.

Why it matters here: This shows a cross-continental teacher-education research consortium built at a scale well beyond a single bilateral exchange, and a working model of how funders now expect joint research and capacity-building outputs, not only mobility, from Africa-Europe education partnerships. It is a useful comparator, and a possible dissemination partner, for the Wits and Aix-Marseille academics working jointly on multilingualism and sustainable development.

Finnish National Agency for Education (EDUFI), Regional Teachers Initiative for Africa, 2025 · Institutional news page of a national education agency coordinating an EU-funded programme

entry.title: Turning chemistry lab experiments into ten 'missions' for engineering and pharmacy students (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the Federal University of Ceará, Brazil, redesigned seven standard General Chemistry laboratory experiments into ten game-based missions, adding experience points, virtual coins and physical rewards. The gamified laboratory ran across five classes of Food Engineering and Pharmacy students, totalling 91 participants, who rated it positively against conventional lab teaching where students simply reproduce fixed procedures. The authors report that gamification is a transformative tool for experimental teaching when paired with clear pedagogical objectives and appropriate technology.

Why it matters here: This is a directly comparable assessment redesign for the Wits project's own laboratory and practical-work components, showing a working points-and-missions structure with real cohort numbers (91 students) rather than a single demonstration class, and a published protocol that could be adapted for metallurgy laboratory sessions on phase identification or mechanical testing.

José Nunes da Silva Júnior et al., Journal of Chemical Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, American Chemical Society (record confirmed via CrossRef)

entry.title: Testing whether a game beats paper for grading hands-on, step-by-step skills (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers from Guangzhou Maritime University and De Montfort University argue that generative AI tools have made memorised, paper-based tests a poor match for assessing procedural, step-by-step knowledge, and tested a gamified alternative instead. In an experimental study with 151 undergraduate students randomly split into experimental and control groups, using a fire-safety procedure as the test case, the gamification-based assessment outperformed the conventional paper-based test at assessing procedural knowledge. The authors argue the approach generalises to assessing procedural knowledge across academic subjects.

Why it matters here: The Wits study is explicitly about assessment beyond the exam, and this randomised, controlled comparison gives quantitative evidence that a gamified assessment can beat a paper test for exactly the kind of step-by-step, applied knowledge that crystallography and phase-transformation work in metallurgy also demands, offering both a research design and a rationale to borrow.

Kun Chen, Shengxiang Yang, Dingbang Luh, Zihao Chen, Honghua Ai and Yi An, Electronics (MDPI), 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (record confirmed via CrossRef)

entry.title: Why African visa rules still carry a colonial charge, a German policy institute argues (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
A briefing from the German institute Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik argues that European visa rules for African applicants still carry colonial-era inequality: it reports that African applicants to Schengen countries faced roughly a 30 per cent rejection rate in 2022 against a 17.5 per cent global average, that the European Union collected about 130 million euros in fees from rejected African applications in 2023, and that African legal migration to Europe fell from roughly 400,000 to 500,000 a year before 2012 to about 270,000 to 290,000 more recently. It illustrates the asymmetry with a Kenya-Germany labour agreement and the fact that Germans can travel to Namibia without a visa while Tanzanians must pay 83 euros and supply extensive documentation.

Why it matters here: For a project designed to move people in both directions between Wits and Aix-Marseille, this is a sober reminder that visa access, not grant funding, is often the real limit on genuine reciprocal mobility, and that the underlying inequality runs one way. It is useful evidence to raise early with the partners' international offices when planning the South to North legs of the exchange.

Franzisca Zanker, Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik, Mobility, Trust and Agency Spotlight 45, 2025 · Policy analysis from SWP, the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, which advises the Bundestag and German government

entry.title: A Mexican university's answer to funding cuts: send students online instead (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
An ethnographic study from Universidad Juarez Autonoma de Tabasco in Mexico describes a virtual exchange pilot run in the first semester of 2024 that paired Mexican students with peers in Greece and Japan, adopted after sustained budget cuts had limited the university's traditional mobility and exchange programmes. Using participant observation of written, image and video contributions, the authors conclude that curriculum internationalisation remained achievable with the resources available, giving students meaningful contact with peers from other cultures without the cost of travel.

Why it matters here: This is a direct account of a Global South institution turning to virtual exchange specifically because funding for physical mobility had been cut, the same budget pressure that limits how many Wits and Aix-Marseille staff and students the Erasmus+ grant can send each year. It offers a concrete, low-cost pilot design that the two schools could adapt for students and staff who miss out on funded places.

Cuevas Álvarez, Pérez Mendoza, Vélez Tellez, Zetina Pérez, Coeto Calcáneo and Alfaro García, Journal of International Students, Vol 15(1), 2025 · Peer-reviewed open-access journal article, Journal of International Students

entry.title: What login patterns and grades reveal about who drops out of Korea's largest online university (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Hanyang Cyber University in Seoul analysed 144,540 student instances recorded between 2018 and 2022, testing logistic regression, XGBoost and light gradient boosting (LGBM) models built from 128 predictors covering demographics, academic records, admissions and learning management system logs. The best LGBM model, trained on eight semesters of data, reached a ROC-AUC of 0.875 for predicting dropout, with age, residential area, occupation, GPA and LMS activity as the strongest signals, and dropout patterns differed by gender.

Why it matters here: This is a directly comparable case at national distance-education scale: a multi-year, multi-semester dataset built from routine administrative and LMS data, exactly the kind PASS aims to assemble from Wits School of Education records, and its comparison of several algorithms and predictor sets offers a benchmark for choosing models and features.

Seo, Yang, Lee and So, Heliyon, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (Heliyon, Elsevier)

entry.title: Qatar University tracks seven years of health-sciences students to see who stays, repeats or graduates (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Qatar University's Health Cluster analysed data on 1,942 first-year health-professions students enrolled between 2015 and 2021 (754 Qatari women, 99 Qatari men, 876 non-Qatari women and 213 non-Qatari men) and trained an XGBoost model that reached 83 per cent accuracy on held-out test data for predicting second-year retention. First-year cumulative GPA and high-school GPA were the two strongest predictors, most students graduated from their health colleges within four to seven years, and retention dropped most for non-Qatari and male students in autumn 2020.

Why it matters here: It shows how a single-institution predictive model for retention can be built from routinely collected admissions and GPA data alone, without new data collection, a low-cost starting point PASS could mirror as it builds its first model from Wits School of Education records before adding richer variables.

Hammoudi Halat et al., BMC Medical Education, 2023 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access (BMC Medical Education)

entry.title: A fairness-audited early-warning model built on Morocco's national school data system (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
The study used anonymised records from Morocco's national Massar education information system, covering 451,852 middle school third-year students in the RSK region, to predict end-of-year pass or fail outcomes about five months before final examinations using first-semester performance data. Nine machine learning models were tested against a hard recall threshold of at least 0.85; the best-performing model, a multilayer perceptron, reached a recall of 0.867 and an AUC-PR of 0.888. An intersectional fairness audit found a persistent gap for male students in rural areas (AUC 0.935 against 0.953 to 0.966 for other groups), and a bias-mitigation step narrowed but did not remove this gap while increasing false positives.

Why it matters here: For PASS, this is a method worth borrowing directly: building a hard recall threshold and an intersectional gender-by-location fairness audit into the model itself, not as an afterthought, gives a template for checking whether a Wits School of Education model works equally well across different groups of students. It is also a rare example of an early-warning system built on a national administrative data system rather than a single institution's data, a useful contrast as PASS begins from School-level data.

El Jihaoui, Abra and Mansouri, Frontiers in Education, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, Frontiers in Education (open access)

entry.title: A six-university Erasmus+ network trains careers and start-up staff across Africa and Europe (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
In May 2026 the University of Ghana announced it had joined a 2026 to 2028 Erasmus+ project led by the University of Münster in Germany, together with Ashesi University, United States International University-Africa (Kenya), Kepler College (Rwanda) and the American University in Cairo (Egypt), to strengthen career development, entrepreneurship training and intercultural learning across Africa and Europe. The project runs staff exchanges, institutional visits, online seminars, workshops and training on start-up development and labour market engagement, coordinated at the University of Ghana by its Careers and Counselling Services Directorate and Innovation Unit. It will also support research into country-specific market opportunities for student-led start-ups.

Why it matters here: This is a live example of a multi-country Erasmus+ staff-exchange network built around a specific professional function, careers and start-up support, rather than a single discipline, a structure the Wits-Aix-Marseille administrative staff mobility strand could borrow directly when designing exchanges for the staff who run the mobility programme itself and its CIVIS link.

University of Ghana, May 2026 · Institutional news page, University of Ghana

entry.title: A machine-learning early-warning system trialled at a Nigerian state university (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Researchers built an early-warning system using academic, behavioural and socioeconomic data from 1,200 undergraduates at Taraba State University between 2023 and 2025, leaving 1,000 valid records after data cleaning. Comparing logistic regression with random forest, the random forest model performed best, reaching 89% accuracy and an AUC of 0.92, with attendance rate, study hours, learning-management-system engagement and parental income the most influential predictors. The authors present the system as a decision-support tool for academic administrators.

Why it matters here: This is a close African peer to PASS in scale and approach: a single Nigerian university building its own early-warning model from routinely collected academic and engagement data, much the same starting point PASS is taking with Wits School of Education data. The predictors it flags, attendance, study hours and LMS engagement, are indicators PASS could test for relevance alongside the data already available through Wits Business Intelligence Services.

Bashiru and Malgwi, Mambilla Journal of Science and the Environment, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, Taraba State University

entry.title: Why South African universities are slow to take serious games seriously (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Writing in the University of Johannesburg's Journal of ExoTechnology and Education, Erna Oliver argues that South African higher education still needs a basic introduction to serious games, and sets out definitions and types of game-based learning for local readers. She concludes that students are ready to embrace serious games and student-centred curricula, but that educators and institutions, accustomed to older teaching methods, are the real obstacle to adoption. The paper was published on 30 November 2025 under a CC BY-NC 4.0 licence.

Why it matters here: As a South African voice on the barriers to serious games, this is a useful check for the Wits study: it suggests that co-design workshops with academics, not just students, may be where the hardest work of introducing gamified assessment in Metallurgical Engineering actually lies.

Oliver, E., Journal of ExoTechnology and Education (JeXed), Vol 1 No 2, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access under CC BY-NC 4.0

entry.title: A continent-wide, geolocated map of nine years of Erasmus+ student exchanges (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Researchers at the University of Helsinki built a geolocated dataset of about 2.3 million Erasmus+ students and 2.2 million individual mobility movements across Europe between 2014 and 2022, geocoded to local and regional units with over 96 per cent accuracy. The data show large cities such as Vienna, Berlin and Madrid keeping a stable balance of incoming and outgoing students, smaller cities fluctuating more, and mobility dropping sharply in 2020 before recovering toward pre-pandemic levels. Regions across Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy and much of Northern Europe emerge as hotspots of diverse student interaction.

Why it matters here: This gives the Wits-Aix-Marseille project a rigorous methodology and a scale benchmark for tracking and evaluating its own mobility flows over its 36 months, and a reminder that even a well-funded scheme like Erasmus+ shows uneven, city-by-city patterns and a sharp shock from external disruption that a small bilateral exchange should plan for.

Väisänen, T., Malekzadeh, M., Inkeröinen, O. and Järv, O., Scientific Data, 2025 · Peer-reviewed open-access dataset article, Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International

entry.title: An open dashboard that turns retention prediction into an administrator's tool (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
A team from Mindanao State University and De La Salle University in the Philippines built EduGuard RetainX, an analytical dashboard that combines academic performance, particularly mathematics and programming grades, admission test scores, GPA, programme and sociodemographic details such as age and sex, to forecast the likelihood that an individual student will withdraw. The dashboard is aimed at institutional decision-makers rather than researchers, and a usability evaluation using a published dashboard-evaluation checklist returned a positive score of 89%.

Why it matters here: EduGuard RetainX is a directly comparable practice piece for PASS: a retention dashboard built and evaluated by a small institutional team, with peer-reviewed evidence of its usability, published openly under a Creative Commons licence through SoftwareX, a journal designed for sharing usable research software. It offers PASS a concrete design precedent for the interface that Business Intelligence Services and the School might eventually build around the predictive model, and a model for how to publish and licence it.

Dia, Sieras, Khalid, Macatotong, Mondejar, Genotiva and Delena, SoftwareX, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (SoftwareX), open access under CC BY 4.0

entry.title: A Tanzanian open university's struggle to reach non-mobile international students at a distance (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
Drawing on interviews with staff at an open and distance-learning university in Tanzania, this article examines how internationalisation at a distance lets non-mobile international students engage with courses without leaving home, at a time when Tanzania positions itself as an expanding international higher education destination. Using the capabilities approach and ideas of conversion factors and third space, the authors identify infrastructure gaps, including unreliable ICT and a shortage of staff with the right skills, as central barriers. They argue that institutions should pool resources and act as a community rather than alone if virtual mobility is to support the SDG 4 goal of broader access.

Why it matters here: This is close evidence on virtual and blended mobility from within the Global South, useful as a comparison for the parts of the Wits-Aix-Marseille exchange that could run online, and as a caution that ICT infrastructure and staff readiness, not just funding, determine whether distance mobility actually reaches students who cannot travel.

Ngalomba, S., Mkwananzi, F. and Mukwambo, P., British Journal of Educational Technology, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article (British Journal of Educational Technology, vol. 56, issue 2), hybrid open access under CC BY-NC 4.0, verified via the University of Glasgow institutional repository record

entry.title: Virtual reality training that teaches mining students to read a mine's machinery (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Researchers at Afyon Kocatepe University's Department of Mining Engineering built a virtual reality training environment in the Unity game engine that lets mining engineering students operate drill rigs, load-haul-dump vehicles and cart transportation systems inside a simulated underground mine. In a usability study, most participants rated the training's benefits at 4.5 out of 5 or higher, while a smaller group who found the VR headset harder to use rated it 3.40 out of 5. The work was published in Mining, Metallurgy & Exploration in October 2024.

Why it matters here: The usability-questionnaire method offers the Wits team a straightforward way to measure how metallurgical engineering students respond to a digital or VR-based game, and the mixed rating pattern is a useful reminder that not every student engages equally well with simulation-based learning.

Gürsoy, M. and Buyuksagis, I.S., Mining, Metallurgy & Exploration, 2024 · Peer-reviewed journal article, Mining, Metallurgy & Exploration (Springer), subscription access

entry.title: A synthetic ore-deposit dataset that lets students play through an entire mine's decisions (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
A team from Luleå University of Technology and the University of Lincoln built a three-dimensional synthetic geometallurgical database of an iron ore deposit so that students could play through decisions across exploration, extraction, mineral processing and site rehabilitation. The tool was presented at the Society of Economic Geologists' 2023 conference in London as part of the EIT Raw Materials 'Emeraldinho' project on hybrid education in Nordic mining value chains. It is released under a CC BY 4.0 licence so that other institutions can reuse the dataset and game design.

Why it matters here: This offers the Wits study a ready model for building a synthetic, structure-property dataset that students explore through gameplay rather than lectures, and shows how a mining and metallurgy value-chain game can be shared openly for other universities to adapt.

Schleret, Tiu, Wanhainen, Jansson, Rosenkranz and Ghorbani, Society of Economic Geologists (SEG) 2023 Conference, 2023 · Peer-reviewed conference proceeding, Society of Economic Geologists, open access under CC BY 4.0

entry.title: A national body runs the analytics and the university runs the support (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Jisc reports that the University of Northampton has chosen its learning analytics service for the whole institution, replacing two separate systems with one, and will extend access to all students from September with full rollout at the start of the 2026 to 2027 academic year. The service combines attendance monitoring, engagement dashboards, reporting and analytics, case management and a student app in one environment. Jisc names Abertay, Bournemouth, City St George's University of London, Salford, South Wales and Suffolk among the other United Kingdom providers already using it.

Why it matters here: PASS is building models from Wits data with the University's Business Intelligence Services, so the interesting part here is the division of labour: a national body supplies the analytics platform while each university keeps the case management and the intervention. It is a live example of the shared-service option Wits could weigh against building everything in house.

Jisc, news item, 20 August 2026 · Announcement from Jisc, the United Kingdom's national body for digital services in tertiary education

entry.title: Seven hundred students across three subjects say what escape rooms actually taught them (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Four researchers at the University of Auckland and Bond University surveyed students and educators about escape room games used in three distinct degree programmes at one large university, and received 708 student responses and eight educator responses. The quantitative answers were analysed descriptively and the written answers by thematic analysis. Students and educators in medical sciences, biological sciences and education all reported rich and many-sided learning, and the authors found that escape rooms promoted similar transferable skills and motivations whatever the disciplinary context. Their recommendation is to use escape rooms sparingly.

Why it matters here: It gives the Wits study a survey design and a sample size to aim at, and its finding that the gains hold across very different disciplines is an argument for trying an escape room in metallurgy at all. The advice to use them sparingly is a useful check on how often a gamified activity should appear in one course.

Kam, M., Clune, M., Jowsey, T. and Singleton, R., Higher Education Research and Development, 2026 · Peer-reviewed journal article, hybrid open access under CC BY-NC-ND

entry.title: Thirty-three thousand Assam student records, and a model that explains why it flagged you (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
Six authors led from Dibrugarh University in Assam analysed 33,627 student records from colleges affiliated to the university, covering students admitted in 2023 and 39 academic and demographic attributes. They compared regression and classification methods and then used explainable artificial intelligence techniques, including SHAP and LIME, to show which features drove each prediction. Logistic regression identified at-risk students with 98.43 per cent accuracy, 99.08 per cent precision and 97.86 per cent recall, and the most influential features were total credit points and overall semester marks, with raised dropout risk below 200 marks and 50 credit points.

Why it matters here: PASS will have to justify to staff and to students why a model flagged a particular person, and this study shows the explanation layer being built in from the start rather than added afterwards. The scale, drawn from affiliated colleges rather than one campus, is also close to the kind of multi-site data a South African faculty would need to pool.

Paul, R., Sarker, S., El Aouifi, H., Hussain, S., Baruah, A. K. and Gaftandzhieva, S., Frontiers in Education, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access

entry.title: A report puts a price on Africa's outbound students and asks who gains (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
This report frames outbound African student mobility as a continental economic question rather than an individual opportunity. It states that more than 460,000 African students leave the continent each year for higher education abroad, at an estimated annual loss of 2.5 billion United States dollars in tuition, innovation and forgone opportunity, and that while 54 per cent of those students are scholarship funded only 18 per cent return. It argues that African countries together spend more on overseas tuition than 25 countries spend on their entire education budgets, and estimates a 500 million dollar annual reinvestment if a quarter of mobile students stayed through hybrid programmes.

Why it matters here: The Wits and Aix-Marseille project sends people out and brings people in, and this is the sharpest available statement of the risk on the outbound side, that mobility can shade into permanent departure. Reading it alongside the project's design is a way of asking what keeps a returning candidate in place, and its figures are a useful counterweight to the celebratory register of most mobility reporting, though they come from a private research group rather than a peer-reviewed source.

Ekanem, K., African Student Mobility Report 2025, Mo-Research Strategy Group, published on Zenodo · Independent research report, openly available on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0, not peer reviewed

entry.title: A mining and metallurgy school built its own simulation game for its own exploration course (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Three staff at the School of Mining and Metallurgical Engineering of the National Technical University of Athens used a design-based research approach to build and evaluate an educational simulation game for probabilistic and spatial reasoning in mineral exploration. The application generates random scenarios in which players direct exploration decisions and end by estimating ore reserves. The game has been adopted as a teaching tool in the course Introduction to Mineral Exploration at the school, and the paper reports game analytics together with a qualitative evaluation drawn from three workshops at higher education institutions in Greece.

Why it matters here: This is the closest published parallel to the Wits study: a mining and metallurgical engineering school designing a game for its own curriculum rather than borrowing one from elsewhere. The design-based research method, and the pairing of game analytics with qualitative evaluation, offer a template for the co-design workshops and classroom observation already planned at Wits.

Valakas, G., Sideri, D. and Modis, K., J, volume 8, article 38, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, open access under CC BY 4.0

entry.title: An Erasmus Mundus master on education, migration and diversity keeps multilingualism as a core module (Erasmus+ mobility with Aix-Marseille)
entry.summary:
EDU_MIG is an Erasmus Mundus master in Education, Migration and Diversity that began taking students in 2025, coordinated by the University of Education Schwäbisch Gmünd with the University of Gävle and the University of Calabria. It offers 25 places a year, a majority of them carrying Erasmus Mundus scholarships that cover tuition, health insurance and a monthly allowance, over two years with mobility between the partner countries. The curriculum is built on three core strands, Migration and Interculturality, Multilingualism, and Educational Sciences, and the network of academic and professional partners runs across Germany, Sweden, Italy, Türkiye and Benin, where students can take internships.

Why it matters here: The Wits and Aix-Marseille project moves master's students in bilingual teaching and academics working on multilingualism, and this is a fully built European programme with multilingualism as a named module and an African partner already inside the consortium. It is worth reading both as a curriculum model for the bilingual teaching strand and as a possible route by which a Wits colleague could join a Mundus consortium later.

EDU_MIG consortium, programme website, first cohort from 2025 · Official programme website of a consortium funded by the European Union under Erasmus Mundus

entry.title: Forty-nine engineering students played a workplace game for four weeks and their empathy scores rose (Gamified learning in metallurgical engineering)
entry.summary:
Three researchers, two of them at Universiti Malaysia Sarawak, tested a serious game called HR Toxic Workplace with 49 engineering project management students at a Malaysian public university. The students played in weekly sessions across four weeks, and empathy was measured before and after with Davis's Interpersonal Reactivity Index, which covers perspective taking, empathic concern, personal distress and fantasy. The study reports significant improvements in empathy, strongest in perspective taking and personal distress, and collected qualitative data alongside the scores.

Why it matters here: The Wits study asks what teaching and assessment beyond the exam can reach, and this is a worked example of a game measuring something an exam cannot: a published instrument, a four-week schedule and a cohort of 49, all small enough to run inside a single metallurgical engineering course.

Techanamurthy, U., Chuah, K.-M. and Yee, I., Australasian Journal of Engineering Education, volume 30, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article

entry.title: Colombia costed its national dropout early-warning system and found it paid for itself (PASS: predictive analytics for student success)
entry.summary:
The Colombian Ministry of Education launched SPADIES, the System for the Prevention and Analysis of School Dropouts in Higher Education Institutions, in 2004 to help institutions collect, analyse and visualise student data, prevent dropout and re-engage students who had already left. Using a differences-in-differences design, the study finds SPADIES lowered dropout probability by 0.7 percentage points, raised on-time graduation by 0.6 points and overall graduation by 0.4 points. The author notes that 0.7 percentage points is roughly 14,000 students, and that the system cost 4.9 million United States dollars between 2005 and 2017 at 2025 prices, about 350 dollars for each student who did not drop out.

Why it matters here: PASS is being built one faculty at a time, and this is what the same idea looks like after twenty years at national scale, with a causal design and a price tag attached. The cost per student retained is the figure a Wits business case would need, and the modest effect size is a realistic expectation to set against the accuracy numbers that prediction papers usually report.

Herrera-Prada, L. O., International Journal of Educational Development, volume 116, 2025 · Peer-reviewed journal article, subscription access
